title: How do you demonstrate internal auditor competence?
description: How to demonstrate internal auditor competence for ISO 9001 and other systems: define criteria, evaluate auditors, keep evidence and monitor audits.
shortAnswer: Internal auditor competence is demonstrated by defining the competence each auditor and audit team needs, covering audit method, the management system standard and sector knowledge, evaluating each auditor against those criteria through training records, observed audits and review of audit reports, keeping that evidence as documented information, assigning auditors so they do not audit their own work, and monitoring audit performance over time, using ISO 19011:2026 as the guidance reference.
keyTakeaways: Certification bodies look for evidence that the organization identified auditor competence requirements, trained to them, and monitors auditor performance.
A lead auditor course certificate shows training, not competence. Observed audits and report quality show competence.
Competence has three parts: auditing skills, knowledge of the management system standard, and knowledge of the processes and sector being audited.
Objectivity and impartiality are part of the evaluation: auditors should not audit their own work.
ISO 19011:2026 (fourth edition, May 2026) is the guidance standard for auditor competence and evaluation. ISO 9001 does not require organizations to use it.

sections.heading: What do management system standards require of internal auditors?

blocks.text: Management system standards require internal audits to be conducted by competent people selected to ensure objectivity and impartiality, and require evidence of competence for people whose work affects the system. ISO 9001 clause 9.2.2 requires the organization to plan, establish, implement and maintain an audit program including frequency, methods, responsibilities, planning requirements and reporting, as quoted in the ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group (APG) guidance on internal audits ([ISO 9001 APG](https://committee.iso.org/files/live/sites/tc176/files/PDF%20APG%20New%20Disclaimer%2012-2023/ISO-TC%20176-TF_APG-InternalAudit.pdf)). ISO 9001 clause 7.2 adds the general competence requirement, including retaining documented information as evidence of competence ([ISO 9001 APG on competence](https://committee.iso.org/files/live/sites/tc176/files/PDF%20APG%20New%20Disclaimer%2012-2023/ISO-TC%20176-TF_APG-Competence.pdf)).

The APG papers were written for ISO 9001:2015. ISO 9001:2026, published on 16 September 2026, retains the Harmonized Structure and clause numbering ([ISO](https://www.iso.org/quality-management/iso-9001-2026)), so internal audit remains in clause 9.2 and competence in clause 7.2. Other standards that use the Harmonized Structure, such as ISO 14001, ISO 45001 and ISO 37301, place internal audit in the same clause. For the competence clause in detail, see [ISO 9001 competence requirements](/regulations/iso-9001-competence-requirements).

Sector schemes can be more prescriptive. The automotive scheme IATF 16949, through a sanctioned interpretation on clause 7.2.3, requires a documented process to verify internal auditor competence and a list of qualified internal auditors ([IATF](https://www.iatfglobaloversight.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/IATF-16949-SIs-Nov-2025.pdf)). See [IATF 16949 competence requirements](/regulations/iatf-16949-competence-and-awareness-requirements).

sections.heading: What will a certification auditor look for?

blocks.text: A certification auditor will look for evidence that you defined auditor competence, engaged trained auditors, monitor their performance, and include sector knowledge on audit teams. The APG internal audit guidance says there should be evidence that the organization has identified the competence requirements for its internal auditors, engages auditors with appropriate training, has a process for monitoring the performance of its internal auditors and audit teams, and includes people on audit teams with appropriate sector-specific knowledge.

The same paper lists objectivity and impartiality of the internal audit process among the issues third-party auditors should evaluate, and asks whether internal auditors understand the risks to the audit outcome if they fail to consider something material, select an inappropriate sampling regime, weight evidence inappropriately or deviate from the audit plan. It notes that ISO 9001 does not require organizations to use ISO 19011, while listing ISO 19011 guidance among the factors to consider.

ISO 19011:2026 is the international guidance standard for auditing management systems, and the reference most organizations use to define and evaluate auditor competence. The fourth edition was published in May 2026, replacing ISO 19011:2018 ([ISO](https://www.iso.org/standard/19011)). ISO describes it as covering the principles of auditing, managing audit programs and conducting management system audits, and lists criteria for auditor competence, evaluation and development among its benefits for auditors. It provides guidance and does not itself lead to certification.

The full text is paywalled, so this guide does not reproduce its clauses. In practice, organizations use it to structure three things: the competence each auditor and audit team needs, the methods used to evaluate auditors, and how auditor competence is maintained and improved. Check your criteria against the 2026 text if your program was built on the 2018 edition.

sections.heading: What are the steps to demonstrate internal auditor competence?

blocks.text: Demonstrate competence in six steps. Each produces evidence an external auditor can sample.

items: **Define competence criteria.** Write criteria for internal auditors in three areas: audit principles and method (planning, sampling, interviewing, evaluating evidence, reporting); knowledge of the standard and your management system; and knowledge of the processes, risks and legal requirements in the areas they audit. Set what a lead auditor needs beyond a team member. See [how to build a competency framework](/guides/how-to-build-a-competency-framework).
**Select and train.** Choose candidates with relevant process knowledge, then train them in audit method and the standard. Record course content and results, not only attendance.

**Evaluate before independent auditing.** Have each new auditor take part in audits under supervision, then lead an audit observed by a qualified lead auditor. Assess against the criteria with a checklist and record the decision.

**Assign for objectivity and sector knowledge.** Assign auditors so they do not audit their own work, and build teams that combine audit skill with knowledge of the process. Record the rationale for each audit team.

**Monitor performance.** Review audit reports for quality, collect auditee feedback, observe auditors periodically, and compare internal audit findings with external audit findings in the same areas. The APG notes that comparing internal results with third-party findings helps evaluate the effectiveness of the internal audit process.

**Maintain and requalify.** Set conditions for staying qualified, such as a minimum number of audits in a period, update training when the standard or your processes change (for example, the move to ISO 9001:2026), and remove people from the qualified list when they lapse.

sections.heading: What evidence shows an internal auditor is competent?

blocks.text: Evidence of competence combines records of what the auditor learned with records of what the auditor did. The ISO 9001 APG on competence notes that participation in a course alone does not necessarily provide evidence that the trainee is competent, and lists evaluation techniques such as observation, peer review, interviews and records review ([ISO 9001 APG on competence](https://committee.iso.org/files/live/sites/tc176/files/PDF%20APG%20New%20Disclaimer%2012-2023/ISO-TC%20176-TF_APG-Competence.pdf)). Use the matrix below.

blocks.text: Keep a qualified auditor list that shows each person's status, scope (which processes or standards they may audit), qualification date and next review. For general audit preparation of training records, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) and [evidence of competence](/glossary/evidence-of-competence).

sections.heading: How can small organizations show internal audit objectivity?

blocks.text: Small organizations can show objectivity by having staff audit areas other than their own, auditing in pairs across functions, or using an external auditor for the areas where no independent internal auditor is available. ISO 9004:2018, quoted in the APG paper, says audits should be conducted by people not involved in the activity being examined, to give an independent view. Record which approach was used for each audit and why.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines auditor competence as a structured framework of concepts, criteria and assessment points linked to the clauses of the standard, so evidence of learning and of performance is recorded against the same criteria. When a standard is revised, the criteria and assessments affected by the change are identified.

faqs.q: Does an internal auditor need a lead auditor certificate?
faqs.a: ISO 9001 does not require any particular certificate. It requires competence and evidence of it. A course certificate is useful evidence of training, but certification auditors also look for evidence of performance, such as observed audits and the quality of audit reports. Sector schemes or customers may set specific training requirements.

faqs.q: Is ISO 19011 mandatory for internal audits?
faqs.a: No. ISO 19011 is a guidance standard and does not lead to certification. The ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group notes that ISO 9001 does not require organizations to use ISO 19011, though third-party auditors may consider its guidance when examining internal audit processes.

faqs.q: Can internal auditors audit their own department?
faqs.a: They should not audit their own work. Management system standards require auditors to be selected so audits are objective and impartial, and ISO 9004 guidance says audits should be conducted by people not involved in the activity examined. Rotate auditors across functions or use external support where independence is not possible.

faqs.q: How often should internal auditor competence be re-evaluated?
faqs.a: Set a review cycle, often annually, and re-evaluate on change: a new edition of the standard, a new scope, or a performance concern. IATF 16949, for example, expects auditors to maintain competence through a minimum number of audits defined by the organization. Remove people from the qualified list if they lapse.
